newsitem.title: UK: Copper ends higher on LME after boomerang trade.
newsitem.headline: Copper ends higher on LME after boomerang trade.

text.p: Copper prices leapt higher during Wednesday afternoon ring and kerb LME trading, with the market doing a 180-degree turn and finishing close to the peaks of the day's $55 range.

Traders said an impressive recovery from a midday nadir of $1,900 was mostly due to shortcovering after earlier speculative selling failed to hit the sub-$1,900 stops. But widening spreads, notably due to tight nearbys, also restored some calm after Tuesday's savage declines.
"All told, it was a classic jobbing market today. Sell it around $1,950 and then look to take it back at the figure ($1,900)," one trader said.
The late upswing faltered at $1,955, and final kerb trade was at $1,950, up $25 a tonne from Tuesday. Cash/threes was at a $34 backwardation by the close, having eased in to $16 this morning.

But despite the smooth recovery from the midsession slump, copper's general trend remains unclear. Given that stocks are at their lowest for six years, with no metal being delivered into warehouses at all, prices should be nearer $2,300, some opined.

"Copper is carrying a lot of baggage around at the moment. There could be some Sumitomo positions still around, we've got options (November declarations) coming up next week, and the Chinese are either buying or selling, depending on who you talk to," another trader said.
Accordingly, short-term trading will remain muddied by uncertainty, with big-volume, large price-swing days on the horizon. "I would not like to call the next $100 move,", an analyst said.

Meanwhile, the increase in UK interest rates was not a market factor, as metals respond more to wider monetary policy moves in the bigger economies, such as the U.S., Germany, and Japan, traders said.

Elsewhere in a lively metals complex aluminium tended to mirror copper throughout the session, easing back to near the $1,400 level, then recovering against a backdrop of some trade buying. Prices finished at $1,428, up $21 from Tuesday.
Nickel spurted higher as well, bouyed by the trend in copper and against a background of talk of possible disruption in New Caledonia, although details were scarce.
Prices pivoted around the $7,300 level at one stage before uncovering some support and chasing up to end the kerb at $7,340 a tonne, against Tuesday's close of $7,325.

The zinc market was heartened by recent upmoves and fund buying, with sentiment also bolstered by the feeling that a big loss-making position originally held by Spain's Asturiana that has hung over the market for some two years has either been liquidated or transferred.
Prices flipped above the $1,050 level in fairly lively late trading to close the day at $1,053, up $11 from yesterday.

Tin business was generally low-key, although a steadier trend was initiated by copper's rally and recent European forward end-user offtake. Last business was at $5,990, a $60 gain from the previous kerb.
Lead similarly moved higher in undramatic trading, but appears to be underpinned by expectations of reasonable battery demand this winter. Final trade was at $748, up $11.
The alloy market was marked higher, and three months closed at a steadier $1,285 a tonne.
